did_you_know.text: Did you know? Job opens the chapter with a personal cry: he says that his soul is weary of life and asks to express his bitterness openly.
Did you know? Job is not content merely to complain; he asks God for a clear explanation: why God contends with him and what charge has caused him to suffer.
Did you know? Job asks why God, who created humanity, seems to oppress him and reject the work of his hands, while at the same time favoring the plans of the wicked.
Did you know? By asking whether God has eyes of flesh and days like those of a human being, Job emphasizes that God does not see and measure reality like a limited human being.
Did you know? Job claims that God knows he is not wicked, but he also understands that he cannot escape God’s hand or find another savior.
Did you know? Job describes his body as the work of God’s hands, but immediately adds that those same hands surround him and may swallow him up and destroy him.
Did you know? The image “You made me like clay” recalls the creation of humanity from dust, reminding God of human frailty and of humanity’s end in the dust.
Did you know? The formation of the body is described through images of milk being poured out and cheese being curdled; afterward come the skin, flesh, bones, and sinews.

Did you know? Alongside his complaint, Job acknowledges that God granted him “life and steadfast love” and watched over his spirit; this recognition highlights the tension between the goodness he received in the past and his suffering in the present.
Did you know? At the end of the chapter, Job describes the land of death as a land of darkness, deep shadow, disorder, and dim light, and asks for a little rest before he goes there.
